---
title: "Baker's dynamic-effects example"
description: "See why one TWFE coefficient need not equal the treated-cell ATT."
jupyter: python3
---

This tutorial translates the public simulation in Andrew Baker's
[JFE_DID](https://github.com/andrewchbaker/JFE_DID) repository. It shows a
specific problem: staggered adoption and cohort-specific dynamic effects can
make a two-way fixed-effects coefficient differ from a natural average effect.

## Data-generating process

The default panel has 1,000 states observed from 1980 through 2015. Fifty
states enter three treatment cohorts:

| Adoption year | States | Effect increase per exposed year |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 1989 | 17 | 0.10 |
| 1998 | 18 | 0.05 |
| 2007 | 15 | 0.01 |

The untreated outcome is

$$
Y_{it}(0)=\alpha_i+\gamma_t+\varepsilon_{it}.
$$

For a state in cohort $g$, the effect grows with exposure time:

$$
\tau_{it}=s_g(t-g+1), \qquad t\ge g.
$$

```{python}
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np

from pypanelsim import designs

config = designs.BakerPanelConfig()
panel = designs.baker(config=config, seed=28101695)

print(panel.shape)
print(panel.truth.att_by_cohort())
```

The outcome matrix contains the state and year effects, while the treatment
matrix shows the three adoption cohorts.

```{python}
#| label: fig-baker-panel
#| fig-cap: "Observed outcomes and staggered treatment in Baker's dynamic-effects design."
#| fig-alt: "Two heatmaps show observed outcomes and staggered treatment after sorting units by adoption cohort."

order = np.argsort(panel.adoption_times, kind="stable")
figure, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 5), constrained_layout=True)
outcome_image = axes[0].matshow(
    panel.outcome[order],
    aspect="auto",
    cmap="viridis",
)
treatment_image = axes[1].matshow(
    panel.treatment[order],
    aspect="auto",
    cmap="Greys",
    vmin=0.0,
    vmax=1.0,
)
axes[0].set_title("Observed outcome")
axes[1].set_title("Treatment")
axes[0].set_ylabel("states, sorted by adoption")
for axis in axes:
    axis.set_xlabel("year position")
figure.colorbar(outcome_image, ax=axes[0], fraction=0.035, pad=0.02)
figure.colorbar(treatment_image, ax=axes[1], fraction=0.035, pad=0.02)
plt.show()
```

## The causal target

The treated-cell ATT gives each observed treated cell equal weight:

```{python}
print("true treated-cell ATT:", round(panel.true_att, 4))
```

It is available without fitting an estimator because the simulation stores the
full causal decomposition.

## The TWFE coefficient

For a balanced panel, residualize a matrix against unit and time fixed effects
by double demeaning:

$$
\widetilde Z_{it}
=Z_{it}-\bar Z_{i\cdot}-\bar Z_{\cdot t}+\bar Z_{\cdot\cdot}.
$$

The coefficient from $Y_{it}=\alpha_i+\gamma_t+\beta D_{it}+u_{it}$ is then

$$
\widehat\beta
=\frac{\sum_{it}\widetilde D_{it}\widetilde Y_{it}}
{\sum_{it}\widetilde D_{it}^2}.
$$

```{python}
def double_demean(values):
    return (
        values
        - values.mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
        - values.mean(axis=0, keepdims=True)
        + values.mean()
    )

d_tilde = double_demean(panel.treatment)
y_tilde = double_demean(panel.outcome)
twfe = float(np.sum(d_tilde * y_tilde) / np.sum(d_tilde**2))

print("TWFE coefficient:", round(twfe, 4))
print("true treated-cell ATT:", round(panel.true_att, 4))
print("difference:", round(twfe - panel.true_att, 4))
```

The difference is not a software error. The regression coefficient uses the
residualized treatment as its weighting object. With staggered adoption,
already-treated cohorts can act as comparisons for later cohorts. Dynamic and
cohort-varying effects then enter with weights that do not match treated-cell
ATT weights.

## Inspect cohort-event truth

```{python}
cohort_truth = panel.truth.cohort_event(event_times=range(0, 8))

for cohort in np.unique(cohort_truth["cohort"]):
    selected = cohort_truth["cohort"] == cohort
    effects = cohort_truth["effect"][selected]
    print(int(cohort), np.round(effects, 2))
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-baker-cohort-paths
#| fig-cap: "True treatment-effect paths by adoption cohort."
#| fig-alt: "A line chart shows a distinct true event-time treatment-effect path for each adoption cohort."

figure, axis = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 5), constrained_layout=True)
for cohort in np.unique(cohort_truth["cohort"]):
    selected = cohort_truth["cohort"] == cohort
    axis.plot(
        cohort_truth["event_time"][selected],
        cohort_truth["effect"][selected],
        marker="o",
        label=f"cohort {config.start_year + int(cohort)}",
    )
axis.axhline(0.0, color="black", linewidth=0.8)
axis.set_xlabel("event time")
axis.set_ylabel("true effect")
axis.legend(title="adoption year")
plt.show()
```

The early cohort has both the steepest slope and the longest observed exposure.
That combination makes the mismatch visible.

## Isolate design from noise

Set `noise_scale=0` to remove sampling noise while keeping the same assignment
and effect structure:

```{python}
noiseless = designs.BakerPanelConfig(n_units=200, noise_scale=0.0)
noiseless_panel = designs.baker(config=noiseless, seed=42)

d_tilde = double_demean(noiseless_panel.treatment)
y_tilde = double_demean(noiseless_panel.outcome)
noiseless_twfe = float(np.sum(d_tilde * y_tilde) / np.sum(d_tilde**2))

print("noiseless TWFE:", round(noiseless_twfe, 4))
print("noiseless ATT:", round(noiseless_panel.true_att, 4))
```

If the gap remains without noise, it comes from the estimand and design rather
than sampling variation.

## What this design does not prove

One simulation does not show that TWFE always fails. It shows a transparent
case where its coefficient and a common ATT target differ. Change effect slopes,
cohort sizes, timing, and noise across replications before making a performance
claim about an estimator.
